newsitem.title: USA: Former official indicted in discrimination case.
newsitem.headline: Former official indicted in discrimination case.

text.p: Texaco Inc.'s former treasurer was indicted Friday for allegedly planning to destroy documents in a highly publicised race discrimination case, the second former Texaco executive to be charged in the scheme.
Robert Ulrich, the retired corporate treasurer, was indicted by a federal grand jury in White Plains, N.Y., on one count each of conspiracy and obstruction of justice.

He is the second former Texaco executive to be charged in the scheme. Richard Lundwall, senior coordinator for personnel services in Texaco's finance department, was indicted in March for obstruction of justice.
The indictment issued Friday is an expansion of the earlier charge against Lundwall and adds one count of conspiracy against him as well.
If convicted, both men face up to 15 years in prison.
The case against the men stems from Lundwall's decision to provide evidence against himself and his colleagues in the racial discrimination case against Texaco.
In a lawsuit filed in 1994, a group of black employees alleged that Texaco discriminated against them in promotions and pay.

Lundwall had secretly taped conversations between himself and others in which they discussed destroying documents requested by the plaintiffs. When Lundwall was dismissed by Texaco in a downsizing move last summer, he gave the tapes to the plaintiffs lawyers.
After the tapes were made public in court proceedings, Texaco agreed last November to settle the case for a record $176.1 million, according to plaintiffs attorneys.

The company also hired an outside investigator who provided Texaco with a report on what had happened at the recorded meetings. Texaco turned the report over to prosecutors, but it was not made public.
After Texaco received the report in January, the company permanently suspended benefits that could be legally cut off to both Ulrich and Lundwall.
The indictment issued Friday states that in May 1994, plaintiffs lawyers in the discrimination case sought certain Texaco documents relating to the promotion of its employees.
Lundwall, Ulrich and others were given the responsibility of collecting the papers, which were to be sent to Texaco's legal department and turned over to the plaintiffs lawyers.

The indictment alleges that in August 1994 Lundwall told Ulrich that certain documents should not be disclosed to the plaintiffs because such disclosure would allow their lawyers to request additional papers and "open doors."
It also alleges that Ulrich directed Lundwall to "shred" and "get rid of" certain documents.
